parts.title: Dr. Lassina Zerbo & Hon. Dr. Jimmy Gasore

segments.text: Thank you. Let me recognize Minister Jimmy and then colleagues, ministers from Africa who have joined us for this Nuclear Energy Summit for Africa. And I also would like to recognize the former minister, my dear friend, Romain Murenzi, who came all the way.

He missed the opening, but I want to recognize his presence. Romain Murenzi is a former minister of science and technology of Rwanda, and we've been working on science diplomacy together for many years. So Romain, welcome.

And I'm sure you've talked about others, and I don't want to start naming all the high level presents in the room, but let me thank you dearly for joining us this year at the NEISA 2026. When we started this, we didn't start it as Rwanda, a country. We wanted to offer a platform where every single African country can take over and then make a case for how involved it could be for nuclear energy implementation.

So we often say one country is taking the lead, but here we all take the lead. And that's why we're talking about rotating this event in the continent so we don't only work together. People see what we can all do together for the continent and by the continent.

Because often when you see conferences, it's somebody else where financing or sponsoring a conference for us to be able to meet. But this has been done by us, for us, and inviting international partners to come and work with us. And I want to, I said it in the opening remark, but I can't stop saying it.

To be able to do that, I have to count on the vision and the leadership of His Excellency President Paul Kagame. When I went to him and then talked about trying to do something for the continent, by the continent, with international partners coming to share their experience, he just said, let's go for it. And we went for it, and here we are.

So in that vein, we have over 1,500 delegates from 58 countries, more than 600 government officials, representatives from over 25 financial institutions. And I want to recognize the African Development Bank. One of the senior advisors here is my dear friend Didier Acouétey
, who has been working in the human capacity building, because that's what he's been doing all his life.

The West African Development Bank, East African Development Bank, the World Bank, and then many FDI. And then Kenya, who has also been showing leadership in a topic that is coming, which is tokenization. And I want to thank them all for being here.

Thank you so much. So what are the key outcomes from the summit? We have a strong recognition that financing nuclear energy in Africa is no longer a theoretical discussion, but an actionable agenda. And it's true, many have told me, but we don't understand, they're telling us it's not an issue of money.

We have money, we can finance. It's a question of making a structure ourselves to make sure people can trust what we want to do. And then when we talk about financing, it's not financing the whole project.

We count on you guys to finance pre-feasibility study, feasibility study, human capacity development, and so on, as we move towards the construction and what could contribute to building or to having a nuclear power plant. The second is a growing readiness from development finance institutions, including the World Bank, as I say, the AFDB, and TDB, to support nuclear-related planning technical assistance. And then I mentioned the feasibility study where they can contribute.

But we've also talked about philanthropy, and then it has been a topic today. And when you see the list of the philanthropic institutions, I would like to see some of our big and main financial gurus, if I could say it in the continent, to join this coalition for the continent so that we don't only see philanthropy from elsewhere coming to help us. We have our own gurus, financial gurus, who can help the young generation move forward for this nuclear energy implementation.

I've talked to the presidents who are present about it, and then they're looking forward to getting some of them to join us. For you, the young people present in the room. So the third is a shared understanding that regional cooperation through interconnected power pool, because we've talked a lot about the electricity power pool, harmonized regulation, shared infrastructure, and joint planning will be essential for scalable nuclear deployment across the continent.

Now since we talk about cooperation, let me lay out some of the things that we've managed to conclude during this NEISA 2026. Cooperation came strongly to the forefront through important announcements and partnership advances during the summit. This includes the Rwanda completion of phase one, where Director General, dear friend Rafael Mariano Grossi, handed over to His Excellency President Kagame, talking about us being at the next phase of the IAEA milestone.

The second is a nuclear cooperation memorandum of understanding between Rwanda and the United States. We have to also mention that we've had several before. We had an understanding with some micro-companies from the U.S. with Rosatom, and then many others.

I also want to recognize the presence of INVAP from Argentina in terms of South-South cooperation. I visited in 2014 Bariloche, the INVAP with their technology that was mainly aimed at helping the developing countries to raise up to the standard of implementation of nuclear energy. It was together with Rafael Grossi at the time, when he was ambassador to the city between the IAEA and Vienna.

So we also have an MOU between the Ministry of Infrastructure, dear Minister Gasore here, and the United States, and the United Republic of Tanzania. An MOU between the Ministry of Finance and the United States, the United Republic of Tanzania. An MOU between the Ministry of Infrastructure and the International Atomic Energy Agency.

We're considering an MOU with GAEC, the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission. That is certainly coming soon, since they're well represented here. We've signed an MOU between RIEB, the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board, and the World Institute for Nuclear Security, WINS.

And then an MOU between RIEB and HALWAL. So I've mentioned, I've recognized Minister Jimmy right in the beginning. Minister Jimmy, I would like you to join me on stage for people to give him a big round of applause for Jimmy's setting, administrative setting, and his personal leadership have been instrumental in making this happen.

So what you see when we say made by us and then for us, it's coming from the Ministry of Infrastructure and Energy. And I often tell Minister Jimmy, he always says, I'm the Minister of Infrastructure, and then I always say, add energy. So maybe what we'll do, since we've hosted this one, Minister Jimmy, you'll start by saying I'm Minister of Energy and Infrastructure.

And I want, before I give to Jimmy, I want to say something. I told President Kagame afterwards when I did this little, I don't know whether it's a joke or whatever, and then he said, Zerbo, this is just a coincidence. I wish it was something that I thought before, but he's glad to see that the coincidence of this thing looks like the atom that represent NEISA for all of you.

So I want to let Minister Jimmy thank those that we have to thank, and then he will close, and then we'll say gracefully thank you to all of you. Jimmy, you have the floor. Thank you, thank you, Dr. Zerbo.

The government of Rwanda decided that infrastructure, energy is part of infrastructure, because energy is the backbone of economic development. So when we set up the Ministry of Infrastructure, often people are surprised it also has energy as infrastructure. So this is not another speech.

I just wanted to thank everyone who joined NEISA 2026. When we look back two years ago, we started very, very small as a small ministerial roundtable. That was December 2024 in a small hotel room here in Kigali.

Then the next one was NEISA 2025, and this one is much, much bigger, NEISA 2026, which now starts turning ambitions and dreams into reality. So I thank everyone who came and joined us, honorable ministers, leaders of international organizations, NGOs, youth and women, we really commend your participation, your contribution, and I'm sure you don't go back home as you came. You learn something and you bring something back home.
Dr. Zerbo gave me credit for the organization of this event. I want to recognize that as a minister, I don't really get to do a lot of things. I follow up and ask questions.

There are so many people, young and women, who worked tirelessly for the last 12 months preparing for this NEISA. I want to recognize the secretariat, the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board, staff at the MININFRA and the government of Rwanda to have made this NEISA a success. So this is not a Rwanda event, it's an African event, and we look to see each other here again next year in Togo.
I think it was already announced. Thank you. And I think, there is to say welcome to Togo
